findings.evidence: attached image-0.png: left panel ticks 0, 100, 200, 300, 400 under identical title text at 0.24..0.50 of the width, right panel ticks 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 at 0.77..0.98; report.py line 350 sets the one xlabel inside the loop over subsets, line 348 sets each subset's own x limit.
findings.summary: The two panels are drawn from one loop with the identical axis title 'Device time per solve [ms]', but their x ranges differ by about twenty times (left to about 430 ms, right to about 22 ms), and nothing inside the panels states that. Only the tick numbers tell a reader the scales are not shared, so a reader scanning across the gap can compare a left-panel position with a right-panel position as if both sat on one axis, and the visual separation of the two columns (x 0.24..0.50 and 0.77..0.98) does not signal a scale break. The caption does state that the panels use separate linear ranges, and every row carries its own tick scale immediately beneath it, so the figure remains readable and the misreading is avoidable by a careful reader; it is recorded rather than blocking.

findings.evidence: attached image-0.png axis titles under both panels; the run's fragment caption at docs/evidence/fragments/sub-millisecond-forward-path/bank-solve-trace-head.html gives 'Device milliseconds per complete sixteen-slice solve'; plan section 3/4 states the per-slice bound.
findings.summary: The axis title reads 'Device time per solve [ms]' without saying that each plotted solve is the sixteen-slice batch total, while the plan this figure informs states its target per slice (sub-millisecond per slice). A reader carrying that target could take the 606 ms batch figure as a per-slice cost, a sixteen-fold misreading of the very quantity the figure exists to report. The caption beneath the figure does say 'Device milliseconds per complete sixteen-slice solve', so the information is on the page; the defect is that the axis that carries the numbers does not carry the normalisation.

rubric_lines: RUBRIC legibility: pass. Two panels of a labelled dot plot. Eighteen source groups carry right-aligned 14 pt names on the y axis, each row showing a grey square (morning trace) and a blue circle (current, the mean of two processes), with one frameless two-entry legend centred above the panels. Tick and axis text is clearly readable at the delivered 1399x720.
RUBRIC data_ink: pass. The ink is 36 markers (18 per panel series, plus two legend glyphs), one baseline per panel, their tick labels and two axis titles. No connecting lines, no fills, no grid.

RUBRIC decoration: pass. No gradient, no background fill, no shaded band, no drop shadow; top, right and left spines are removed and the y tick marks have zero length, so each panel carries only its bottom scale.

RUBRIC contrast: pass. Axis and tick text measures 7.9:1 against white (median glyph pixel 82,81,78). The grey square series is #929292 at 3.11:1, above the 3:1 floor for a non-text data mark, and the blue circle series is #1f5d92 at 6.91:1. No text or mark is lost to lightness.

RUBRIC table_form: pass. The image carries a paired magnitude comparison across 18 categories sorted by size, which is a comparison a reader scans rather than looks up; the exact per-group milliseconds and shares are already supplied as an HTML table in the fragment, so the figure is not an image of that table.

RUBRIC label_collision: pass. No text is clipped: all dark text pixels lie within x 61..1372 and y 18..677 of the 1399x720 canvas, and zero dark pixels fall in the outer 3 px frame on any edge. No label overlaps another label; the closest label-to-marker approach is 10 px (right panel, the rows at or below about 1 ms, where the marker sits just inside the plot's left limit), and paired markers in one row are 16 to 17 px apart centre to centre with about 10 px glyph height, so no two marks touch.
